1.goal: To open with the sentence this whole block was built around: she has already used this verb nine times.
1.interaction: T speaks; S listens. Thirty seconds, then move.
run: Say it, in these words: she already used this verb nine times, in the first two lessons.

Say why it matters, if she asks: in the consultation she named this verb as the proof that she was behind — if I do not even know the verb to be. Seeing that she was already using it changes her relationship with the whole course.
Do not turn it into a speech. One sentence, and move on.
exact: The opening sentence, verbatim: "You already used this verb nine times, in the first two lessons."
1.expected: Surprise, or disbelief. Either is the right reaction and neither needs an answer.
1.support: If she does not believe it, point forward: the six sentences on screen 3 are hers.
1.challenge: Ask her to guess which verb it is before you say it.
1.monitoring: How she reacts to being told she already does something she said she could not do.
1.evidence: Her reaction, in her own words. It is the thing the block set out to change.
1.transition: Move on once she has heard it.

2.goal: To take the baseline before any input — three sentences about herself, unprompted.
2.interaction: S speaks alone; T writes down what she says.
run: Ask for three sentences about her — anything.
Write down what she says, word for word. This is the baseline the rest of the lesson is measured against.
CORRECT NOTHING HERE. Not a word.
exact: The prompt, and nothing after it: "Three sentences about you. Anything."
2.expected: Three sentences, however broken. Fragments count as attempts and get written down as fragments.
2.support: If nothing comes, give the opening of the first one only: "I am…" Then wait, and stay quiet.
2.challenge: Ask for a fourth about someone else in her family.
2.monitoring: Which forms appear on their own, and which are missing. Do not react to either.
2.evidence: The three sentences exactly as she said them. This is half of today's evidence, and it is taken before any teaching.
2.transition: Move on when the three have come out, however crooked.

3.goal: To put her own sentences from lessons 1 and 2 in front of her, and let her see three forms in them.
3.interaction: S classifies on screen, T checks.
run: The sentences on screen are HERS, from lessons 1 and 2. If you wrote down the real ones, use the real ones.
She classifies the six.
CCQ: how many different forms are there here? (Three: am, is, are.)
Do not name the verb yet. It gets its name at stage 5.
3.expected: Six classified, and the answer three to the CCQ.
3.support: If she is stuck, cover everything but the marked word and ask again.
3.challenge: Ask her which of the three forms she used most, and why she thinks so.
3.monitoring: Whether she recognizes the sentences as her own.
3.evidence: Whether seeing her own production changes what she says about her level.
3.transition: Move on when the six are classified.

4.goal: For her to find what changes — before anybody gives her a rule.
4.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: She marks the three correct sentences.
Then ask, in Portuguese if you need to: what is different about the three that are wrong?
DO NOT GIVE THE RULE. It comes at stage 5.
Give her own formulation back in English, without turning it into a rule.
exact: Giving her formulation back: "Yes — the form changes with the person in front of it. Say that back to me in English."
If nothing comes, the two options: "Is it the verb that changes, or the rest of the sentence?"
4.expected: In her own words: the form does not match the person in front of it.
4.support: If nothing comes, offer two options and let her choose.
4.challenge: Ask her to fix the three wrong ones out loud.
4.monitoring: Whether she reaches the generalization herself. This is the pedagogical center of the lesson.
4.evidence: Whether she can state the pattern before being told it.
4.transition: Move on when she has said what changes.

5.goal: To show the table once, AFTER she has already tried — not before.
5.interaction: T shows and reads with S. Two minutes, no more.
run: Show it, read it with her, and move on. Two minutes.
CCQ: My children ___ at home — which one? (are.) And Breakfast ___ included? (is.)

If she says she does not know grammar, answer ONCE and move on: today she did not learn a new rule, she gave a name to what she was already using. Insisting turns this into a subject in which she is behind.
exact: The one answer to "I do not know grammar": "You did not learn a rule today. You gave a name to something you were already doing."
5.support: If a CCQ misses, point at the row of the table rather than explaining it again.
5.challenge: Ask her to make the negative and the question of one of the two CCQ sentences.
5.monitoring: Whether the table lands as a confirmation or as new material. It should be a confirmation.
5.evidence: What she says about her own grammar when the table appears.
5.transition: Move on when both CCQs are answered.

6.goal: To run twelve short sentences fast, so the form stops needing a decision.
6.interaction: T gives the subject, S completes. Fast, no pauses.
run: Twelve sentences, quickly. You give the subject, she finishes.
Correct gently and immediately, in one word. No explanation.
COUNT THE HITS — this is half of today's evidence.
exact: The subjects, one after another with no pause: "I…" / "My hotel…" / "My children…" / "Breakfast…" / "You…" / "It…" / "My daughter…" / "They…" / "We…" / "The room…" / "My husband…" / "I…"
The correction, one word only: "is." And then straight to the next subject.
6.expected: Twelve completions. Anything at or above nine is fluent enough for stage 7.
6.support: If she stalls three times in a row, slow to one every four seconds and keep going. Do not stop to explain.
6.challenge: Run the last four in the negative.
6.monitoring: The hit rate, and where the misses cluster — are with plural subjects is the usual one.
6.evidence: The number of hits out of twelve. Half of today's evidence, and the number stage 8 is compared against.
6.transition: Move on when the twelve have gone by.

7.goal: To move from the drill to her own content, with the table still on screen.
7.interaction: S speaks, T corrects. The table stays open.
run: She says her six sentences with the table still visible. Here you still correct.
If she wants to talk about her family instead of the trip, take it — true content is worth more than the topic on screen.
Three positive, two negative, one question to you.
7.expected: Six sentences of her own, with the table available.
7.support: Point at the row of the table rather than saying the form.
7.challenge: Ask for a second question, this one about you.
7.monitoring: Whether the negative and the question cost more than the positives.
7.evidence: What she chooses to say when the content is hers.
7.transition: Move on when the six have come out.

8.goal: The same six, live and consecutive, with nothing on screen.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are someone she met at the hotel.
run: CLOSE THE TABLE.
Six sentences in a row, nothing on screen: three positive, two negative, one question to you.
DO NOT CORRECT DURING. Write down the hit rate — it goes against the drill, and the pair is the result of the lesson.
exact: Opening, in role: "Nice to meet you. Tell me about yourself."
If she stops, the first word and nothing else: "I am…" / "I am not…" / "Are you…"
8.expected: Six sentences without the table. The question to you is the one that usually goes missing.
8.support: Give the first word of the frame and wait.
8.challenge: Answer her question and ask one back, and see whether she keeps going.
8.monitoring: The hit rate without the table, against the hit rate in the drill.
8.evidence: The two rates, side by side. At her level a number is the only honest way to see progress across three lessons.
8.transition: Move on when the six have come out.

9.goal: To give back one thing, say the two numbers out loud, and ask for the same six about someone else.
run: One thing, not two.
Say the two numbers out loud — hits in the drill and hits in the free speech. At her level, seeing a number is the only honest way to see progress across three lessons.
Then the same six about her daughter or her son. I am becomes she is, and that is where everybody slips.
exact: Saying the numbers: "Nine out of twelve with the table, and seven out of twelve without it. Three lessons ago that number was zero."
Opening the retask: "Now the same six, about your daughter."
9.expected: The six with she is where I am used to be, and the rest of the sentence unchanged.
9.support: If the subject change breaks the sentence, give the first two words and let her finish.
9.challenge: Ask for one of them in the negative as well.
9.monitoring: Whether the change of person takes the whole sentence down with it, or only the verb.
9.evidence: What happens to the sentence when the person changes. It decides what lesson 4 has to carry.
9.transition: Move on when the six have come out about someone else.

10.goal: To close on what she discovered today, not on what she learned.
10.interaction: T–S. She ticks what she recognizes.
run: She marks what she recognizes on screen.
Close on the discovery and not on the content: she was already using the verb she had named as the proof that she was behind.
Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about her family and two reference pages.
Announce lesson 4 — it closes the block: the whole check-in, from good morning to thank you, with one question she has not seen.
Lesson 4 reads the four records together. Fill in today's before you close.
exact: Closing on the discovery: "You did not learn this verb today. You found out you were already using it."
10.expected: Some of the items ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could say tomorrow.
10.challenge: Ask which of the three forms she trusts least, and note the answer.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence row moved since lesson 1.
10.evidence: The two hit rates, her confidence reading, and what she said when she saw her own sentences on screen 3.
